activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
The argument started at 9:42 on a Sunday night, which was when Ekam typed "Told you. Best game by a QB all season" into the chat and attached a screenshot of a stat line. Bryce replied within a minute, saying the stat line was garbage because the guy threw for most of it in the first half when the other team was already asleep. Grayson read both messages twice, then a third, because he had homework open in the next tab and this was far more interesting.

"A game isn't one number," Bryce wrote. "You're boiling down sixty plays into a screenshot."

Ekam came back with something about how the number existed, it was official, and screenshots didn't lie. Grayson noticed that Ekam's screenshot had a number next to the quarterback's name, 143.7, with no explanation attached, and that neither of them had said what the number actually measured. That bothered him more than the argument itself. He opened a new tab and typed the number in, then the words "NFL passer rating."

The first thing he found was a page saying the passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3. Grayson stared at that for a while. A perfect game, apparently, was not a 100. It was 158.3, a number that looked like it had been assembled from spare parts. He thought about how rankings and averages in general did this, mashing a whole bunch of separate things into one verdict that people then argued about as if it were a single fact. He decided to test whether Ekam even knew what he was posting.

"Ekam," he typed, "if the guy had a perfect game, what number would the screenshot show?"

"100," Ekam wrote back instantly. Then, "obviously."

Bryce sent a single crying-laughing emoji, which did nothing to hinder the argument and possibly helped it. Grayson pasted the link. He watched the typing indicator bounce at the bottom of the screen for a long time, the three dots appearing and vanishing like something elastic being stretched and released. When Ekam finally answered, it was just "ok that's a weird number," with no period, which meant he was typing on a phone and was annoyed.

"He still had the best game," Ekam added.

"Based on one number that you thought maxed at 100 until ninety seconds ago," Bryce wrote.

Grayson leaned back. His homework was still open in the other tab, untouched, and his mother had said something earlier about lights out at ten that he was now on the wrong side of. He typed one more message, took a screenshot of the clock, and sent it.

"Verdict: Ekam's guy had a great game, Bryce won the argument, and nobody knows what 143.7 means. Good night."

The dots bounced again. Ekam replied, "one more thing," and attached a highlight video that was eleven minutes long.

Grayson watched the first ten seconds of it under his blanket.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The Panic of 1837 caused a long economic depression in the United States, and many ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land.
story:
Livia pressed her nose close to the glass case in the old trading post at Fort Laramie's restored visitor center. Behind the glass lay a diary, its pages brown as dried apples, its ink faded to the color of weak tea. Her worksheet had one question on it: use a primary source to explain why this family moved west in the 1840s. She had copied the diary's transcription onto a card, and now she read the last line again. "The bank has taken the farm, and there is nothing left for us here."

"Is that even a primary source?" Cashton asked, leaning over her shoulder. "It's just a copy on a card."

"It's a copy of one," Livia said. "The diary is the source. It was written by the person who was there. That's what makes it primary."

Ariana read over Livia's other shoulder, chewing the end of her pen. "But it doesn't say why they left. It just says the bank took the farm. That's not a reason to walk two thousand miles into buffalo country."

Livia turned the card over. On the back, the museum had printed a note about the exhibit, mentioning that the laser scanner in the back room was used to preserve fragile pages so that visitors like her could read them at all. She stared at the diary line again. "They lost the farm," she said slowly. "That's the thing we can't see directly. We see the trail, the wagons, the lush green river valleys they were headed toward. But the reason is back east, in a bank ledger."

"So test it," Cashton said. "You're always saying that."

She looked around the room. Mr. Bighorn, the guide, stood near the door in his ranger hat, answering a tourist's question about oxen. Livia walked over, card in hand. "Mr. Bighorn, this family lost their farm to the bank. Did that happen to a lot of people, or just them?"

He shook his head. "Happened all over. They called it the Panic of 1837. It caused a long economic depression in the United States. Ruined farmers all across the country, and a lot of them later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land."

Ariana had followed and was writing fast. "So it wasn't just one family being unlucky," she said. "It was a wave."

Livia went back to the case and knelt down so the diary sat at eye level. The glass smelled faintly of cleaning spray, and beyond the window she could hear wagon ruts being pointed out to a school group on the trail below. She read the line once more. The bank has taken the farm. Then she wrote her answer on the worksheet: the family risked the dangerous trail because the Panic of 1837 had ruined them, and cheap, fertile land waited at the other end.

"Nice," Cashton said, reading over her arm. "But look at the date on the next page."

Livia turned the card. The next entry was dated a month later, and the handwriting had changed. It was smaller, and it began, "Since Mother died on the Platte, Papa says we do not speak of the farm anymore."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.
story:
The blue-and-white vessel on Mr. Tang's shelf had been there since September, and on Monday morning it lay in three pieces on the floor. Mr. Tang didn't yell. He just wrote one question on the board: "What happened here?" and said the class would discuss it after lunch.

Nathaniel spent lunch in the library, because he intended to solve this before the discussion started. Somebody had knocked the vessel down between Friday afternoon and this morning, and whoever it was had said nothing. He found a folded note tucked in his library book, in Milla's looping handwriting: "I was last in the room Friday. I saw Ines by the shelf. Don't tell anyone. Something's weird about the pieces." Nathaniel read it twice, then folded it small and pushed it into his pocket.

Ines, it turned out, had her own plans. During the discussion she stood up and told the class that the vessel had already been cracked on Thursday, that she had seen a thin black line running through the painted birds, and that the real question wasn't who broke it but why nobody reported a dangerous shelf. Mr. Tang asked who else had seen the crack. Four hands went up, and then the room exploded.

"I saw Ines bump the shelf," said one boy. "I saw the cat from the hallway jump," said another, and half the class laughed because there was no cat. A girl insisted the vessel had simply slid, that the shelf wasn't level, that she'd noticed the birds weren't symmetrical anymore, tilted wrong, all week. Mr. Tang wrote each version on the board, one, two, three, four, and Nathaniel stared at the four contradictory stories until his ears hummed. Four witnesses, four versions, one broken thing. Something about it tickled at him.

Then Milla raised her hand. "My dad showed me an old movie last month. Rashomon, from 1950. It's about one crime, but four witnesses tell it and every story contradicts the others." She shrugged. "I keep thinking about it because nobody's lying exactly. They just saw it differently."

"That's what's happening here," Nathaniel said slowly, and then he stopped, because something cold moved through him. The note in his pocket. The blue thread he'd found near the pieces, the exact blue of his own backpack strap. Friday afternoon, hurrying out, swinging his bag over his shoulder. He had been standing right there by the shelf. He thought about it and thought about it, testing it against every version on the board, and only one version had a boy with a blue backpack in it, the girl who mentioned the sliding shelf, and the boy had been him.

"Ines didn't bump it," Nathaniel said, standing. His voice came out steadier than he expected. "The shelf wasn't level either. It was me, and I didn't even know until right now. I think my backpack hit it Friday when I left." Mr. Tang picked up one of the three pieces and turned it over in his palm.

"Then you'd better fix it," he said, and held out the glue.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Avoiding everything that causes anxiety brings quick relief but often makes the anxiety stronger over time, because the person never learns the situation is manageable.
story:
The group chat had been quiet for two days, which was strange, because the Science Fair Chat was usually chaos. Andrew lay on his bed scrolling up to find out why. There it was, from Albert: "Reminder, presentations start Monday, order circulates tomorrow." Below it, Lawrence had typed "cool" at 9:14 p.m. and nothing since. Andrew knew what nothing since meant. Lawrence had a whole system: when he was anxious about something, he stopped talking about it, hoping it would disappear. It had worked in October, when a stomachache got him out of the book report. It had worked in December, when his internet "went down" during the history slideshow. But Andrew noticed something the grown-ups seemed to miss. Each time Lawrence dodged a presentation, the next one seemed to scare him more, not less. In October he'd been nervous. By December his hands shook when the teacher just said the word slides.

Andrew typed, "Lawrence you alive?" Three dots appeared, then vanished. Then appeared again. "yeah. busy."

"busy doing what"

"stuff"

Andrew stared at the screen. He tried to imagine the chat from Lawrence's side, and the picture that formed was bleak: a boy sitting in a quiet house, refreshing the thread, waiting for Monday to be canceled by magic. Avoiding the thing brought Lawrence quick relief, Andrew figured, the way pulling your hand off a hot stove did. But somehow the anxiety got bigger every time, because Lawrence never got to find out the presentation wouldn't kill him. Andrew wasn't sure that was a real rule, but he had a way to test it. He'd skipped his own piano recital in November by faking a cough, and the spring recital had felt ten times worse. Maybe the rule ran both directions. Maybe the only way out was through.

He called Lawrence instead of texting, because texting let you hide. "Order circulates tomorrow," Andrew said when Lawrence picked up. "Want to sign up for the same block? I'll go first, so if I bomb it, you'll know the ceiling won't fall in."

"You don't get it," Lawrence said. "My anxiety is like, an actual thing. Ms. Berg said coping means finding what works for you, and what works for me is not doing it."

"That's not coping, that's a trap with good lighting," Andrew said. "Also I checked the rubric. Delivery is one criterion out of five, and it's the smallest one. Your volcano data is so good you could present it in a paper bag."

There was a long pause, the kind that used to make Andrew hang up. This time he waited. "The deadline for topic changes is ambiguous," Lawrence said finally. "It says 'before the fair,' which could mean tonight or never."

"So change it to something you actually want to talk about. You pick, I'll handle the sign-up sheet. Boundaries, remember? I'm allowed to say you can't hide in this chat forever."

Lawrence sent a volcano emoji, then: "fine. but if I throw up on the projector, you're explaining it to Ms. Berg."

Monday morning, Lawrence's hands still shook, but he stood up there anyway, and afterward he sat down fast, like a man escaping a wave. In the chat that night he wrote, "she said my data was the strongest in the class." Then, a minute later: "next time I might not even fake a stomachache."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: At a bar or bat mitzvah, the young person often also chants the haftarah, a reading from the books of the Prophets.
story:
Joshua had been practicing his Torah portion for two months, and he still couldn't get through it without stumbling, which was why he was standing in the cemetery on a Saturday morning, talking to a headstone. "Zayde," he said, "it's the part where the melody jumps that provokes me into rushing. I rush, and then the whole thing falls apart." The granite said nothing, but it was quieter here than anywhere, and his grandfather had always said quiet was where the words finally stuck.

Samuel had come along, mostly out of curiosity, and now stood on the gravel median between the cemetery lanes, spinning in slow circles. "You know you're saying it wrong, right?" Samuel called. "Not the melody. The amount. Rayne told me her brother chanted a second reading at his bar mitzvah."

"A second one?" Joshua's stomach dropped. He counted on his fingers. He had learned the Torah portion. He had not learned anything else.

"From the Prophets," Samuel said. "It's called the haftarah. Her brother complained about it for a year."

Joshua sat down on the cold grass beside the headstone and thought about his grandfather. Zayde had come here every Sunday morning for as long as Joshua could remember, long after his own father had died, and he had always come home calm. Joshua had assumed it was grief. Now he wondered if it was something else. He pulled out his phone, found the haftarah for his date, and pressed play on the chanting recording.

The voice rose and fell over the rows of stones. A groundskeeper, Mr. Owusu, came down the lane with his rake and paused to listen. "That's a new one on me," he said. "You mourning or rehearsing?"

"Rehearsing," Joshua said. "Probably both." He played the recording three more times, then stood, planted his feet like his grandfather used to plant them, and chanted the first line himself. His voice cracked on the high note. He tried again. The crack moved. On the third try, the line came out whole, and it hung in the air like something visible.

"It's probable nobody chants perfectly the first day," Samuel said from the median.

"I know." Joshua was already scrolling to the next line. The wind moved through the grass, and somewhere behind the oldest stones a cardinal called twice, as if keeping time.

"Same time next week?" Samuel asked.

"Same time," Joshua said, and began again from the top.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
story:
Lincoln sat cross-legged on his bed with his notebook open to a blank page. The amendment project was due tomorrow morning, and all he had was a title and one sentence about the First Amendment that he had crossed out twice. His phone buzzed with a message from Rayna: "Started mine yet?" He typed back "halfway," which was a lie, and put the phone face down on the blanket.

The problem was not the assignment itself. He could draft a paragraph about the Fourth Amendment in ten minutes if his hands would stop jumping to his phone. Every few minutes his anxiety spiked, small and specific: the deadline, the blank page, the group chat where Angela was posting about the quiz they had both bombed. His stress had a shape today, like a stone in his shoe he could feel but not see.

He tried an experiment on himself. He set a timer for fifteen minutes and wrote without stopping, phone in the drawer. At minute six he caught himself reaching for the drawer anyway, hand in midair. He put the hand back on the notebook and kept writing. At minute twelve the sentence about search warrants came out whole and correct, and he underlined it. Something invisible had loosened, and he wanted to know what.

He called Rayna. "How do you get through a bad day?" he asked. "Actually get through it, not just survive it."

"Walks," she said immediately. "My mom calls it coping. It means the ways you handle stress or difficult feelings. Mine are running, going to bed on time even when I don't want to, and calling you, apparently."

Lincoln was skeptical. "A walk fixes nothing."

"I didn't say fixes. I said handles. Big difference. What's yours?"

He looked around the bedroom, at the drawer with the phone in it, at the screen glowing through the crack. "Scrolling, mostly. And staying up until one."

"Those sound like the opposite," Rayna said. "Try the walk and the sleep tonight, then tell me how the project goes. And stop texting me when you're supposed to be writing. That's a boundary, Lincoln."

He hung up, half annoyed and half curious, and did the math out loud. He had been handling the stress with the phone and midnight hours, and he had one sentence to show for three days. Rayna had been handling hers with movement, sleep, and talking to people, and she was, by her own report, actually halfway done. Same stress, different methods, different results. That was a pattern, and it repeated, and repeating was what made it a rule rather than luck.

He went outside and walked twice around the block in the dark, hands in his jacket pockets, no phone. The cold made his thinking narrower and cleaner, like a windshield after the wipers pass. Back upstairs he wrote two full paragraphs on the Fourth Amendment, set his alarm for ten instead of one, and put the phone to charge across the room.

At 9:58 the phone buzzed one more time. Angela: "you up? quiz stress is eating me." He picked it up, typed "walk tomorrow before school, meet me at the corner," and set it down. Then he turned off the lamp and pulled the blanket to his chin.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Friendships usually fade without contact, so friends who move apart and stay close tend to keep in touch regularly through calls, messages or visits.
story:
The new house echoed so loudly that Alexa's sneakers squeaked twice on every step. She had claimed the bedroom at the top of the stairs, even though it was completely bare, and she stood in the middle of it now with her phone in her hand. Downstairs, the moving truck was already rumbling toward her old neighborhood, where Cashton and Jenson were probably sitting on the curb doing nothing.

"Alexa!" her mom called. "The pizza's here!"

Alexa didn't move. She was thinking about her cousin Marisol, who had moved to Arizona three years ago and whom she now had almost nothing to say to. That had felt like some bizarre slow magic at the time, like Marisol had been erased a little at a time. But Alexa had started noticing a pattern last week, flipping through old messages. Marisol had called twice after the move, then once, then never. Her friend Priya, who'd moved to Ohio in fourth grade, still texted her every Saturday morning without fail, and they were as close as ever. Same situation, opposite result. The difference had to be something she couldn't see, some hidden cause, and she thought she'd found it: friendships fade without contact, but the ones that survive moving are the ones where people keep in touch regularly, with calls, messages, or visits. Priya had contact every single week. Marisol had almost none.

It was like erosion, Alexa thought, chewing her pizza at the kitchen counter. Water wears rock away slowly, and nothing dramatic happens, and then one day the cliff is gone. Well, she could eliminate that possibility for Cashton and Jenson right now, tonight, before school started and everything got busy.

She ran back up the echoing stairs and called their three-way group. "Before you say anything," she announced when Cashton's face appeared, "I have a plan. Sunday nights, seven o'clock, video call, all three of us, every single week. Non-negotiable."

"Every week?" Jenson said. "That's a lot of weeks."

"That's the point. Priya and I have done it since fourth grade and we're still tight. I'm not losing you two to slow fade-out." She paused. "So, is it a deal or not?"

Cashton held up his hand to the camera, palm out. "Deal. Sunday, seven. And Alexa, when you find a skate spot in the new town, you call us that same day, even if it's a Tuesday."

"Especially if it's a Tuesday," Alexa said, and pressed her palm flat against the cool screen.

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: In 1837, ornithologist John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, some of which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were a new group of closely related finches.
story:
Nicolas crouched by the back fence with his notebook open, watching the bird feeder he had built from scrap wood and a plastic bottle. His problem was simple and annoying: for his science project he needed to describe how natural selection had shaped the beaks of finches on different islands, and every time he tried to write it down, the words turned to mush. He figured that if he could actually observe birds competing for food in his own backyard, the whole idea would become something he could see instead of just recite.

His prototype feeder had two stations. One held small seeds behind a fine mesh that only slender beaks could reach, and the other held big sunflower seeds in the open, better for thick, strong beaks. It wasn't robust yet; the mesh sagged and the wind knocked the whole thing sideways whenever a sparrow landed hard. He had spent Saturday morning fixing it with zip ties and a brick.

Anita arrived with her bike helmet still on. "What are you doing?"

"Testing beaks," Nicolas said. "Watch. The little birds go for the mesh side. The bigger ones crack the sunflower seeds."

A chickadee zipped in, grabbed a tiny seed through the mesh, and left. A cardinal followed and hammered at a sunflower seed until it split. Anita leaned on the fence. "So that's your whole project? Birds eating?"

"It's the Galápagos thing," Nicolas said. "Different islands, different food, so the finches' beaks ended up different shapes, because the ones whose beaks fit the food survived and had chicks."

Yohan came through the gate next, carrying a granola bar, and immediately pointed at a brown bird pecking under the feeder. "That's a wren."

"It's a finch," Nicolas said.

"Looks like a wren to me," Yohan said. "Or maybe a blackbird."

Anita laughed, and Nicolas felt his ears go hot, because honestly he wasn't sure either. He went inside and came back with his library book, the one with the chapter about Darwin. He flipped pages until he found it and read aloud.

"In 1837, this ornithologist, John Gould, told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, some of which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were a new group of closely related finches."

Yohan blinked. "Wait. Darwin got them wrong? The Darwin?"

"Collecting them himself," Nicolas said, "and he still thought some were wrens or blackbirds, and Gould was the one who figured out they were all finches. Closely related finches."

Yohan actually smiled. "Okay, then I don't feel bad." He settled onto the grass. "So the birds on the different islands all came from one group, and the beaks changed island by island?"

"That's what I have to show," Nicolas said. He looked at his feeder, then at the notebook, and began sketching two islands with different plants on them, arrows showing which beak shape won out on each. "I can integrate my feeder data as the backyard version. Small beak, small food. Big beak, big food. Same rule, smaller scale."

Anita tapped the mesh side. "You'll need to fix this before Monday if you want it to hold up for the demonstration."

They spent the next hour rebuilding the weak side with a sturdier frame, testing it by pressing down with a stick. The mesh held. A sparrow landed, worked a seed loose, and flew off, and Nicolas wrote "trial four, frame held" in his notebook.

Yohan pointed at another brown bird near the fence. "Finch or wren?"

"Finch," Nicolas said. "Probably."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The cell wall is the thick outer border you see around each onion cell, making the cells look like rows of bricks.
story:
Jayden had budgeted exactly four minutes of the science period for the microscope, and eight for labeling his diagram, because the worksheet was due at the end of class and Ms. Yamamoto did not accept late work. He clipped a thin layer of onion skin onto his slide, added the drop of stain the way the instructions said, and pressed his eye to the eyepiece. The light hummed. Then he froze, because what he saw was not cells at all. It was a brick wall.

Rows and rows of rectangles, pale and stacked, stretched across the circle of light like a garden wall somebody had photographed from above. He sat back, checked the slide, and looked again. The wall was still there. He raised his hand halfway, then lowered it, because Allie at the next station was already laughing at her own eyepiece.

"Jayden, I think somebody put a brick wall in my onion," she said. "Like an actual tiny brick wall. Is that possible?"

"It's not a brick wall," said Nael, who had finished early and was wandering past with his notebook. "Those bricks, each one is a cell. The whole cell."

Jayden looked again. Each rectangle had a thick outer border, darker and heavier than anything inside it, and it was that border that made the shapes look like bricks in the first place. If each thick-outlined box was one single cell, then the border itself had to be the cell wall. That left the thin dark smudge near the middle, which could only be the nucleus, and the faint line just inside the outer border, the membrane. He felt the pattern click into place, quiet and certain.

He tested it. On the lowest magnification the rows looked like bricks; when he turned the knob to high power, the shapes swelled and the thick border of one cell filled half the view, which would never happen with an actual brick wall. "Try your fine focus," he told Allie. "Count how many rectangles are across one strand of the skin. If it's a wall, the count should change when you move the slide. It won't, because you're counting cells."

Allie nudged her slide a hair to the left. The same rows slid past, brick after brick, cell after cell, unchanging. "Okay," she said slowly. "Every single one of those is a whole cell. That's a plague of cells."

"That's an onion," Jayden said, and started drawing his rows of bricks.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: The placebo effect is when people feel better after a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill, simply because they expect it to help.
story:
Elijah slid the mashed potatoes toward Katarina, who was too busy talking to serve herself. "Two whole seconds faster," she said for the third time. "I timed both laps. The only thing I changed was Volt Rush. I drank half a can before the second lap and I flew."

Elijah's dad passed the green beans and asked what was in the can. Katarina read from her phone: caffeine, taurine, something called L-theanine, and fifteen grams of sugar. "See? Real ingredients. Real results."

Elijah chewed slowly. He had a science fair presentation due in two days, and his poster board was still blank in his closet. His teacher, Mr. Leung, had told the class that a claim needed tested evidence, not just one person's story about one person's experience. Katarina's two seconds were exactly that, a story. But there might be a project hiding inside it.

"Here's my problem," he said. "You presume the drink made you faster because the drink was different. But other stuff was different too. Second lap, you were warmed up. You'd already run it once." He set down his fork. "You know what would actually test it? If you drank Volt Rush before your first lap one day, and before a lap another day when the can actually had something else in it."

Katarina frowned. "Like what else?"

"Like sugar water. Same taste, same can, no active ingredients. If you still get faster, it wasn't the caffeine doing the work. It was you expecting it to help." He pulled out a notebook and wrote "Day 1" and "Day 2" in his neatest printing. "My dad can fill one can with sugar water and seal the lid. Neither of us tells you which day is which until after both laps."

"Wait," Katarina said. "I've been telling everyone at track about Volt Rush. Blakely already bought three cans with her allowance." She pushed the potatoes around her plate. "If I get faster on the fake one, I'm going to feel pretty dumb."

"You'll feel like a scientist," Elijah's dad said, standing to refill his water glass. "Dumb is refusing to check."

The next afternoon they met at the track with Blakely holding the stopwatch, since her whole purchase was on the line too and she wanted to see it through. Elijah handed Katarina a can from a paper bag. She drank, ran her lap, and Blakely called out the time: 74.2 seconds, a hair under her old first-lap pace. Two days later came the second can, and this time Katarina crossed the line at 73.8. Blakely checked the stopwatch twice, then checked Katarina's face. "That's faster than Tuesday."

Elijah opened his notebook and showed Katarina the list his dad had written: Day 1, Volt Rush. Day 2, sugar water. She stared at it, then laughed so hard she had to sit down on the track. "The plain water day was the fast one? I got faster off sugar water and believing in it?"

"There's a word for it," Elijah said. "Mr. Leung told me it's called the placebo effect." He underlined it in his notebook and started sketching the poster in the margin. "The good news is you own two whole seconds of speed that came out of your own legs. That's a pretty stable result. You could probably keep it."

"At least until I find out what was really in the cans," Blakely said, still holding the stopwatch like evidence. "How do I get a refund on three of these?"

Katarina stood up, brushed the rubber off her hands, and jogged back toward the starting line. "Timer ready," she called over her shoulder. "One more lap, no can at all."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 33 of the Canadian Charter, the notwithstanding clause, lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights for up to five years, and the override can be renewed.
story:
Kayla slid her library book across the table so fast it knocked over Theresa's juice box. "Okay, presentation is Friday. Mr. Ong says we each pick one right from the Charter and explain it in our own words. I want the best one."

"There is no best one," Theresa said, mopping the spill with her sleeve. "They're all, like, you can vote, you can move around, nobody can search your locker."

Gabriela leaned in, smelling of the vinegar from her science project, where she was counting decomposers in a jar of dead leaves. "My brother says there's a weird one in the news. Something about the government being allowed to break the rules."

"That can't be true," Kayla said. But it snagged in her mind all afternoon, and at dinner she asked her dad, who shrugged, so on Saturday she went to her grandmother's house, where the radio was always on and somebody was always arguing about something. Sure enough, her uncle was waving his coffee at the kitchen table. "They used it again," he was saying. "That notwithstanding clause."

"The what?" Kayla asked.

Her grandmother tapped the newspaper. "Section thirty-three. It lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights. But only for up to five years. Then they have to do it again if they want it to keep going."

"Wait." Kayla grabbed a pen from the junk drawer. "They can just switch off a right? Like a light switch?" She wrote fast, her grandmother holding the paper steady while the kettle shrieked behind them.

"Five years," her uncle said, "and then they can renew it. That's the part that bothers me."

Kayla read her notes three times on the bus home, testing an idea. If a right could be switched off, then rights weren't like gravity, inevitable and fixed. They were more like the school dress code, rules that people in charge had voted on and could vote on again. And if that was true, then the list in the Charter was less a wall and more a promise, and promises had to be watched. She felt the thought click into place the way a lock does.

On Friday morning she asked to go first, before the presentations that would precede lunch and everyone's attention would collapse. She stood at the front with her one page of notes. "My right is freedom of expression. But here's the twist. Section thirty-three, the notwithstanding clause, lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights for up to five years, and they can renew it. So I checked what my right actually is. It's not a shield nailed to the sky. It's something we keep choosing." She held up her page. "In my own words: my right exists as long as I pay attention to it."

Mr. Ong stopped writing and looked up. "Say the last part again."

"My right exists," Kayla said, "as long as I pay attention to it."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law, passed in 2009, was the first U.S. state law requiring that a young athlete with a suspected concussion be removed from play until a health professional clears them.
story:
Cameron sat at the kitchen table with his cleats still on, mud drying on the laces, while Thea scrolled through her phone across from him. On the fridge behind her hung his older brother's jersey, which had always seemed to symbolize the family's idea of a real athlete, and Cameron had spent all of yesterday's tryouts trying to prove he deserved one of his own.

"You should have seen Tobin," Cameron said. "He went up for the header, came down wrong, and just sat there for a second with this blank look. Then he stood up and told the coach he was fine. He kept saying it was tryouts, that if he sat out he'd lose his spot." Cameron turned his water glass in slow circles. "The coach pulled him anyway. Tobin was furious. Honestly, so was I. It seemed unfair, like the coach was punishing him for getting hurt."

"I don't think coaches can just decide that," Thea said. She spun the phone toward him. "Look. Type his name or something." Cameron took the phone and became a scavenger, hunting through article after article, most of them useless, until he found what looked like the probable source of the coach's decision.

He read it out loud, slowly, making sure he had it right. "Washington's Zackery Lystedt Law. Passed in 2009. It was the first U.S. state law requiring that a young athlete with a suspected concussion be removed from play until a health professional clears them." He read the last part twice. "Until a health professional clears them. Not the coach. Not the player." He leaned back. "So the coach wasn't choosing anything. He had to pull Tobin, no matter how much Tobin argued. And Tobin can't go back until a doctor says so."

"So it wasn't unfair," Thea said. "It was the rule." Cameron nodded, though something still bothered him. He thought about his own header in the second drill, the way the ball had clipped the side of his head and his ears had rung for a moment, and how he had shaken it off and kept playing because tryouts only came once a year. He hadn't told anyone. He wasn't even sure it had been anything. He looked at his reflection in the dark kitchen window, then back at the phone, then at the mud on his cleats.

"There's open practice next Thursday," he said. "Tobin's going to try to sneak back in before he's cleared, I know he is." He picked up the phone and started typing a message to him. "Not happening without a fight."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double with compound interest: divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate, so about 12 years at 6 percent.
story:
Edouard spread the papers across the kitchen table: two bank statements from his father's old account, a calculator, and a notebook with Caden's phone number scrawled on the cover. Caden wanted fifteen dollars for their share of a used skateboard ramp, and Edouard had exactly nine. He had told Caden Saturday. That gave him four days.

The account had two pages side by side. One showed simple interest, five percent, five years. The other showed compound interest at the same rate, and the numbers drifted apart, small at first, then wider. Edouard tapped the calculator. He wrote both ending amounts in his notebook and stared at them. Same rate, same years, same starting money. Something invisible was working in the second column, something he couldn't see in any single line. He flipped back and forth between the pages like the answer might fall out.

He called Caden. "Simple gives you the same dollars every year," Edouard said. "Compound pays interest on the interest."

"So?" Caden's voice was flat.

"So compound wins. Over five years, look, it's more. Not a radical difference, but more." He read the two totals down the phone. He heard Caden's chair creak.

"I need the fifteen by Saturday, Edouard."

"I know." He hung up and went back to the table.

His mother passed through with laundry. "Still at it?"

"How long would money take to double? At, say, six percent."

She set the basket down. "Your grandfather used the rule of 72. Divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate. At six percent, about twelve years." She picked up the basket again. "He liked that trick."

Edouard ran it. Seventy-two divided by six was twelve. Twelve years. He would be twenty-six when his savings doubled. He wrote his age beside the number, then drew a box around it. His one lazy neuron finally firing, Caden would say. He tested it against the statement: at five percent, seventy-two divided by five was about fourteen years to double. He checked the compound column with the calculator, year by year, and the answer held close. The rule worked.

He salvaged what he could from the drawer of his desk: three crumpled dollars, two quarters, and a five he had forgotten in an old birthday card. Ten fifty. He counted it twice. Then he texted Caden: "I have ten fifty. You cover the rest, I build the whole ramp alone."

The reply came back fast: "Deal. Bring the hammer."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms became part of Canada's Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982.
story:
George pressed his finger against the glass case in the courthouse lobby and read the bottom of the Charter poster for the third time. "Proclaimed on April 17, 1982," he muttered. "That's not even that long ago."

Oakley leaned in beside him, fogging the glass with his breath. "Why do you keep staring at the date? Ms. Tehrani just said we had to explain one right in our own words by Friday. She didn't say anything about dates."

"Because it's weird," George said. "My grandpa was already alive in 1982. My dad was seven. So what did they have before it?" He wrote the date on his palm with a pen, because his notebook was buried in his bag and Ms. Tehrani's class was in twenty minutes.

In the classroom, Ivory noticed the smudged ink on his hand right away. "You wrote on yourself again?"

"Look," George said, and held out his palm. "The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It became part of Canada's Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982. So before that date, no Charter. My grandpa came here in 1975. What rights did he even have?"

Ivory shrugged. "Maybe there was something else."

"Maybe. Or maybe nothing written down like this." George had a theory forming, the way he did when a math problem looked impossible and then turned out to have a pattern hiding in it. His idea was simple: if he asked his grandpa what it was like before the Charter existed, the answer would tell him what the Charter actually did. You couldn't see a right, but you could see the hole where it used to be missing.

That evening he called his grandpa, who laughed at the question and then didn't laugh. He talked for a long time about arriving before 1982, about things he could not contest, about being turned away and having no paper to point to. "Now you point to it," his grandpa said. "Section fifteen. That one took years to fully kick in, even after." George wrote down section fifteen, equality rights, and underneath it his own sentence: everybody gets treated the same by the law, no matter who they are, because it's written down and you can demand it.

On Friday he read his sentence aloud, and Ms. Tehrani asked him where he had found such a strong explanation. "My grandpa," George said. "He tested it his whole life."

After school, Oakley found him at his locker. "Your grandpa sounded pretty sad on the phone, though."

"He was," George said. He shut the locker and looked at the date still faint on his palm, half washed away. "The words came in 1982. Everything else is still catching up."

He pulled his sleeve down over the smudge and walked out.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Musical loudness is marked with Italian words: piano means soft and forte means loud.
story:
Emily had one week to learn the middle section of "March of the Silver Bells" before Friday's assembly, and the paper in front of her was full of tiny letters she didn't understand. Between the notes, printed in italics, were the letters p, then f, then p again, scattered like someone had spilled alphabet soup across the staff. When she played the passage through, it came out flat and steady, the same volume all the way to the end. Ms. Haddad had said the piece needed "shape," and shape was exactly what Emily couldn't find.

She took the sheet music to lunch and spread it out at the table between her tray and Alaric's. "These letters," she said, pointing. "What are they even for?" Alaric leaned over, chewing, and squinted at the p and the f. "No idea. Maybe they're leftover from an old version. Some kind of obsolete marking they forgot to erase." Emily frowned. Composers didn't usually forget things. If the letters were printed there, on purpose, in a pattern, then they probably meant something the same way every time.

After school she carried the music to the practice room, where Greta was already at the second piano. Emily had an idea she wanted to test. She would play the passage twice, once ignoring the letters completely and once changing something at each one. On the first run she played everything at the same comfortable volume, and it sounded like a radio stuck between stations. On the second run she made a guess: f for fast and loud, p for soft and slow. The p sections suddenly shrank into something quiet and careful, and the f sections bloomed. It wasn't right yet, but it wasn't flat anymore either.

Greta looked up from her own music. "What did you just do? It actually sounded like a march." Emily slid the page across. "The little letters. I think they tell you how loud to play. Watch." She played the phrase at f, full and ringing, then dropped to p so gently that the last note barely touched the string. Greta tried it herself, then grinned. "My cousin had a book about this. She used to say it all the time. Piano means soft and forte means loud." Emily looked down at the page, and the scattered letters turned into a map. Every p was a valley. Every f was a hill.

By Thursday evening she could play the whole middle section without stopping, swelling and shrinking where the letters told her to. On Friday she sat at the school piano in front of the whole assembly, hands poised over the keys, and waited through Ms. Haddad's nod. When the march began, the quiet part came out so soft that the first row leaned forward to hear it, and then the f arrived like a door swinging open. In the third row, Greta was mouthing the letters along with her, p and f, p and f, all the way to the final chord.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, all lines going straight back into the distance meet at a single vanishing point on the horizon line, at the viewer's eye level.
story:
Jonathan spread his paper across the kitchen table and pinned it down with the salt shaker. He was drawing Main Street for the art contest at school, the one Ms. Cardinal had announced on Friday, and he wanted his street to look like a photograph, like you could walk right into it. So far it looked like the street was melting. The left edge of the road angled toward one corner of the page. The right edge angled toward another. The sidewalk lines went off in a third direction entirely, and the whole drawing had a counterfeit depth to it, like a stage set instead of a real place.

He called Vincent, who was entering the contest too. "Draw the road like train tracks," Vincent said over the phone. "Tracks get closer together farther away." Jonathan tried it, narrowing the road toward the middle of the page, but the buildings still leaned at each other like drunks. When he hung up, his little sister's toy sailboat sat on the table, and out of frustration he sketched it, its hull curving, the mast straight. It looked more solid than anything on his street. The problem wasn't his buildings, he realized. It was the lines that ran back into the distance. They were disagreeing with each other.

Cedric came over after lunch, and they dragged the kitchen chair to the front window to look down their own street. "Look at the curb," Jonathan said. He held a ruler up at arm's length, squinting one eye, and lined it up with the curb as it ran away from them. Then he did the same with the roofline of the Hendersons' fence and the edge of the sidewalk. "They all point at the same spot. The far end of the street, right at eye level."

"Eye level?" Cedric said.

"That's where the horizon line is," Jonathan said. "And every line going straight back meets at one point on it. Vanishing point." He said it out loud mostly to hear whether it sounded crazy. It didn't. It sounded like a rule, the kind you could test.

Back at the table, he drew a flat horizon line across the paper and marked a single dot on it. Then, ruler down, he ran every receding edge of the street, the curbs, the sidewalk seams, the rooflines, straight to that dot. He even set the toy sailboat on the porch of one of his buildings and angled its lines to match. The buildings snapped upright. The street lay down and went somewhere.

He held the drawing at arm's length and looked at it with one eye, the way he had looked at the real street. "Tomorrow we draw the windows," he said, tapping the dot. "Right here, all of them, every single one."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A heritage language is one spoken at home or in the family that differs from the main language of the wider community, and heritage speakers may speak it without reading it.
story:
Carson had joined the after-school club mostly because his mother said he couldn't just come home and play games every afternoon, but he stayed because of the board by the door. Everyone in the club had taped up an index card with a word or phrase from a language spoken in their house. Juliana's card said "goodnight" in Portuguese. Jaida's had three lines of curly script Carson couldn't begin to sound out. Mr. Sok's card, oddly, had only English.

At the first meeting, Mr. Sok asked them to share one word they knew from home. Juliana rattled off a sentence in Portuguese, smooth as anything, and Jaida answered her grandmother on the phone every Sunday in that curly language, laughing and arguing and shushing the dog. But when Mr. Sok asked who could read their word out loud from their card, only Juliana's hand went up. Jaida squinted at hers and admitted she'd copied it by shape, like drawing a picture, and couldn't check if she'd gotten it right.

"It's a heritage language," Mr. Sok said. "Spoken at home, different from what the whole neighborhood speaks."

That was the sentence that got Carson thinking on the bus home. So a language could live in your ears and your mouth but not in your eyes? He turned it over all evening, the way he'd puzzle out why the garage sensor only flashed when the cat crossed it, not the mail carrier. His best guess was approximate, not certain: speaking and reading were separate skills, and if nobody ever taught the reading part, you could still chat away. How would he test that?

The next week he brought a folded note and slid it across the table to Jaida. In it he'd written, "Can you read this?" in English, and below it, "Can you read what your grandmother writes in her cards?" He watched her face while she read. She smiled at the first line, then stopped at the second, and her ears went pink.

"She writes me a card every birthday," Jaida said quietly. "I always say thank you and hug her, and I have my cousin read it to me later when nobody's around. I fake the moment." She looked at the note again. "Is that what you figured out? That I talk but don't read?"

"Sort of," Carson said. "I wanted to see if the rule held. And it does, I think. So here's my real question. Want to fix it?"

They budgeted their time, twenty minutes at the end of every club meeting, and Juliana joined in because she liked puzzles. Mr. Sok dug up a workbook, and Carson made flashcards, and Jaida started with the letters in her own name. By the last meeting before winter break, she opened a card from her grandmother, moved her finger slowly under each word, and read the whole thing out loud to the club, all the way to the end, which said, "You are my whole heart."

"Next year," Jaida said, "I'm writing one back."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: SUM skips cells that hold text, so a number stored as text is silently left out of the total.
story:
The spreadsheet was supposed to be the easy part. Wyatt had spent two days collecting prices for the class fundraiser bake sale, typing every muffin and cookie into column B while his partner Melodie collected the same list from the other half of the class. Now, in the computer lab, he clicked into B14 and typed =SUM(B2:B13), pressed Enter, and got forty-one dollars. The bar chart Mr. Haile had asked for glowed on the next screen over, showing one bar towering over eleven others, and it looked less like a fundraiser and less like anything sane.

"That can't be right," Wyatt said. "The chocolate chunk alone was twelve dollars."

Melodie leaned over. "Then it's right. That's mostly what we sold."

"No, the total. Forty-one. But the bars add up to way more than that." He pointed at the chart, where the column for Thursday's cookie sale stretched up like a giraffe at a pony party.

Mr. Haile walked past their row on his way to fix the printer, which had been intimidating the substitute all period. He glanced at their screen, said nothing, and kept walking. Wyatt suspected this meant the answer was something he was supposed to find himself.

He clicked on B9, the twelve-dollar chocolate chunk cell. In the formula bar it said "12, with a little apostrophe in front that he had never noticed before. He checked the other cells. Some had it, some didn't, and when he added up the ones that didn't, in his head, he got forty-one exactly.

"I typed mine," Melodie said, watching him. "You pasted yours from the message your dad sent."

"So pasting did something." Wyatt didn't know what, but he had an idea. He deleted the apostrophe 12 and typed a plain 12, then hit Enter. The total jumped to fifty-three. The bar chart updated too, the chocolate chunk bar suddenly matching its neighbours instead of sulking near the floor.

"SUM skips cells that hold text," Wyatt said, mostly to himself, watching the numbers move. "So a number stored as text just gets left out."

"Which is quietly evil," Melodie said.

He went down the column, retyping every pasted number. While he worked, he thought about the flyer they'd make afterward, the one with prices, a chart, and a small note about how the money would help, since even contemporary bake sales had to worry about inflation raising the price of butter. When he typed the last cell, the total read ninety-two dollars, and every bar stood where it should.

He hit print and walked over to stand beside the printer, arms crossed, waiting to see if it would try anything.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: The climax is the turning point of a story, the moment of highest tension when the main conflict is decided one way or the other.
story:
Jacob sat at the kitchen table with his draft spread in front of him, a story about two brothers racing homemade boats across the pond behind their house. His assignment was due Monday: a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax. The dialogue he could handle. The climax was the problem.

"So which scene is it?" Christopher asked, leaning over the pages. "The part where the boat sinks, right?"

Xavier shook his head. "No way. It's the fight the brothers have on the dock. That's the loudest part."

They had come over after school to help, and now all three of them were arguing about a story Jacob had written himself, which felt strange, like arguing about his own handwriting. He read the draft again, and something snagged in his mind. The fight scene was loud, sure, but after it, the brothers still weren't done with each other. Nothing had been decided yet. He wondered if loud was the same as important, or if those were two different things entirely.

"Wait," Jacob said slowly. He flipped to the last page, where the younger brother finds the older one's boat floating upside down near the reeds, half translucent under the water, the rudder snapped clean off. "The climax is the turning point of a story, the moment of highest tension when the main conflict is decided one way or the other. Not just the loudest part."

Christopher frowned. "So the sinking?"

"It's this," Jacob said, tapping the paragraph where the younger brother has to choose: grab the boat and lose the race, or keep racing and let his brother's work sink for good. "Everything before it could still go either way. After it, the answer is set."

Xavier read the paragraph twice, lips moving. "Huh. So the fight was just... buildup?"

"Setup," Jacob said, though he wasn't fully sure that was the right word either.

He picked up his pencil. The paragraph needed dialogue, and the punctuation rules from Ms. Ngo's handout ran through his head: quotation marks around the spoken words, comma inside the quotes before the tag, new paragraph each time the speaker changes. If his character wouldn't comply with those rules, the whole page would fall apart, and Ms. Ngo had already circled three comma errors on his last draft in red pen. He wrote carefully, erased, wrote again.

Christopher read the new lines out loud, testing them. "Sounds like real people talking."

"Yeah," Xavier said. "But you changed the ending. Now he just stands there holding the boat. Is that on purpose?"

Jacob looked at the final line, where the younger brother waits at the finish line with the broken boat in his hands, watching the water and not saying anything. He hadn't planned it that way. The pencil had gone somewhere he didn't expect.

"Maybe the reader decides," he said, and turned back to the page.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Checking in privately afterward with a classmate who was teased, and telling them it was not okay, can help them feel less alone even if nobody stepped in at the time.
story:
At fencing practice on Thursday, Frankie would not leave Darian alone. Darian had missed an easy parry three times in a row, and Frankie kept calling him "rodent boy" because of the way he tucked his chin when he lunged. "Look at him," Frankie said to the whole gym, loud enough that even Mr. Tanaka paused at the equipment rack. "Rodent boy can't keep his head up."

Jack stood in the on-deck line with his mask under his arm, watching. He wanted to say something, but he could picture exactly how it would go: he'd snap at Frankie, Frankie would snap back, and pretty soon they'd be the show instead of Darian. Then everyone would circle around, and Darian would stand there being humiliated in front of an even bigger audience. Jack knew that pattern from last year, when a kid named on the bus had ended up in a worse spot because someone defended him with a joke that turned into a roast.

So he tried the other thing first, the quiet thing. He stepped onto the strip and said, "Frankie, you're up with me. Mr. Tanaka's watching footwork today." It wasn't a rescue. It was just a fact that pulled Frankie's attention sideways. The teasing stopped because there was suddenly a bout to think about, and Mr. Tanaka did start calling out footwork corrections, and the gym moved on. Darian got through his drills without another word aimed at him, though Jack noticed he kept his mask on longer than he needed to.

Jack felt strange about it on the walk to the water fountain. He hadn't exactly done nothing, but he hadn't exactly done anything either. He ran the situation back in his head like a slow-motion replay. Darian had heard every word. Nobody had said it wasn't okay. If Jack had been the one getting called rodent boy in front of twelve people, what would stick with him afterward, the name, or the silence from everyone else?

He tested the idea after practice. He waited until Darian was unlacing his shoes by the lockers, away from the group, and sat down on the bench a few feet away. "That stuff Frankie was saying," Jack said. "It wasn't okay." Darian didn't look up right away. His hands kept working at the laces. "Nobody said anything," he said finally. "I know," Jack said. "That's why I'm saying it now." Darian pulled the second shoe off and set it beside the first, neat and deliberate, like he was buying himself a second to answer. "It helps," he said. "That you came over. Weirdly it helps."

They walked out together past the equipment rack, where Mr. Tanaka was winding cords. "Same time Saturday," Mr. Tanaka said, not looking up, and Jack thought maybe he had noticed more than he let on. Outside the gym doors, Darian said, "Next week I'm keeping my chin up." Jack bumped his fist against Darian's bag. "Rodent boy retires," Darian said, and grinned.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: A microscope's total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective lens power, so a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective magnifies 400 times.
story:
Lily had been waiting all semester for the microscope lab, and now that the moment had finally arrived, she was stuck behind Brodie, who was arguing with Adele about who got the station by the window. The science museum's lab smelled faintly of vinegar, and on the counter sat a tray of onion slices, tweezers, and slides. Mr. Chowdhury had said the first team to label a correct sketch of an onion cell would get to tour the electron microscope in the basement, and Lily wanted that tour more than anything.

"Split the difference," she said, sliding between them and claiming the stool. "I'll cut the specimen, Brodie loads the slide, Adele draws. We all win." Brodie grinned and peeled a paper-thin layer of skin from the onion with the tweezers, dropping it onto the glass. Lily added one drop of iodine, mindful of the hygiene rules posted on the wall about not touching faces with stained gloves, and pressed the coverslip down.

Adele leaned over the eyepiece first. "It's like little bricks," she reported, pencil already moving. "I can see the walls. But I can't find the nucleus anywhere, and the membrane looks wrong." Lily peered in. Under the lowest lens, the cells were faint outlines, pale gray and barely worth sketching. She twisted to the next objective, and the cells sharpened, but something was off. They were far too small to be magnified properly, and Adele insisted that was impossible because the lens, she claimed, magnified fifty times.

"Fifty?" Lily checked the barrel. Stamped on the objective it said 40x, and on the eyepiece, 10x. She remembered Mr. Chowdhury's worksheet line about total magnification: the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective lens power. She did the math in the margin of Adele's sketch. Four hundred, not fifty. "You're only counting one lens," she said. "It's four hundred times."

"Then the nucleus should be here somewhere," Adele said, tapping the drawing. Lily turned the fine focus very slowly, one hair's width at a time, holding her breath. The pale gray deepened to gold. In the center of a cell, a dense little dot rose out of the blur like a stone surfacing in a pond. "There," Lily whispered, and Adele circled it and wrote nucleus in careful letters.

Mr. Chowdhury walked past their station, glanced at the labeled sketch with its wall, membrane, and nucleus, and stopped. "Basement tour," he said. "Three o'clock." Brodie pumped his fist, and Adele carefully tore the page free, because after the iodine dried the onion skin would turn brittle and the slide would be ruined anyway. Lily slid off the stool and said, "I call first look at the electron microscope."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Naive realism is the belief that we see the world as it really is, so people who disagree with us must be uninformed or biased.
story:
Mr. Ross set a timer on the board before the discussion even started. Twelve minutes, he said, and by the end every group had to agree on one sentence describing what happened in the photograph he handed out. The photo showed a man standing beside an overturned cart of oranges in the middle of a street, a small crowd gathered around him, nothing more. Alex looked at it and thought the answer was obvious.

"His cart tipped and people are helping," Alex said, sliding the picture to the middle of the desk. Neriah shook her head before he finished. "Look at their faces. They're arguing. Maybe he knocked over somebody's cart and they're mad." Salman leaned in, tapping the corner of the photo. "There's a scratch on the wall behind him. I think a car hit the cart and he's yelling at the driver." Alex frowned. Three people, one picture, three different stories, and each of them talked as if the others just hadn't looked properly. "You can't see a car," Alex said. "You can't see helping," Neriah said.

Alex tried an experiment. He flipped his notebook to a blank page and wrote, in careful letters, what each of them thought the people in the crowd wanted. Neriah's crowd wanted to help or to blame. Salman's driver had a motive to leave the scene. His own crowd had no motive at all, just an accident. When he read the three lines side by side, something clicked. Each of them believed they were seeing the photo as it really was, and so the others had to be wrong somehow. He raised his hand before he could talk himself out of it.

"Mr. Ross, is there a name for that? When you think you see things exactly as they are, so anyone who disagrees must be uninformed?" Mr. Ross paused at the board, then smiled. "Naive realism," he said, and wrote nothing else, leaving the timer ticking. Five minutes left.

Alex turned back to his group. "We're all doing it. We each think the picture is obvious and the other two are just missing something." Salman started to argue, then stopped, and looked at the photo again for a long moment. "Okay," he said slowly. "I can't actually see a driver." Neriah crossed out something in her notes. "I can't see arguing either. Faces aren't proof." Alex picked up the pen. One sentence, all three of them watching, thirty seconds on the clock.

They wrote: "A cart of oranges tipped over in a street, and why is something people could see differently."

The timer buzzed, and Neriah laughed first.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, a program only needs to test odd divisors, because an odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one.
story:
Ella typed 999,331 into her prime checker and hit run. The little wheel in the corner of the screen spun. It kept spinning.

"Ms. Rodríguez says our programs have to finish before the bell," Archie said from the next computer. "That's four minutes."

"I know." Ella watched the wheel. Her program tested every number from 2 up to 999,331, one at a time, asking each one: do you divide evenly into 999,331? It had already churned past 400,000. She could tell from the counter she'd added, a number climbing so fast it looked like static.

Kali leaned over from the far row. "Mine finished in two seconds for 999,983."

"Then yours is wrong."

"Yours is slow." Kali turned her screen. Her loop stepped by two. "After 2, I only try odd numbers."

Ella frowned at it. "That skips half the checks. You'll miss a divisor."

"Think about it. 999,331 is odd. Can an odd number split evenly into groups of four? Or six? Or any even amount?"

Ella pictured it. Nine hundred thousand marbles, poured into buckets of four. Every bucket of four used up an even number of marbles, so the leftovers stayed odd all the way down. There would always be one marble left over. She grabbed a scrap of paper and wrote 15 divided by 4. Three remainder 3. Then 21 divided by 6. Three remainder 3. Then 15 divided by 5, which came out to exactly 3. She sat back. "Okay. Okay, odd only."

She changed one line. Instead of going up by one each time, her loop jumped from 2 to 3 and then stepped by two, 3, 5, 7, 9, all the odd numbers. She ran it again. The counter climbed, but the work had been cut in half, like a plateau she'd been climbing face-first when there had been a stair around the side. The wheel spun for one second, not four minutes.

"Prime," the screen printed.

"Prime," Kali confirmed, checking her own output.

Archie's counter was still grinding past 700,000. He looked at Ella's finished screen, then at his own, and his shoulders sagged. "Show me the line," he said. "Before the bell."

Ella copied the scrap of paper onto his desk, the arrow and the step-by-two, and slid it over. "You have to move this," she said, pointing. He dragged the line into place and hit run, and the three of them watched his screen as the spinning wheel vanished and the answer surfaced from the opaque gray of the waiting screen, sharp and small: Prime.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: Green or yellow mucus comes from immune cells and an enzyme they release, so its color alone does not show whether an infection is caused by bacteria or a virus.
story:
Michael had been stationed on the living room couch for three days, surrounded by a box of tissues, a blanket, and two crumpled napkins that had migrated under the coffee table. His cold was almost gone, but that morning he had blown his nose and seen something that made his stomach drop. Green. Bright, unmistakable green on the tissue.

He held it up to the window light, then folded it quickly when his mom walked past with soup. Once she was in the kitchen, he unfolded it again and stared. Green meant infection, and infection meant he might need medicine, maybe even a shot. He imagined missing the school talent show on Friday, where he and Vanessa were supposed to perform their juggling act. Vanessa had already texted him four times asking if he was still coming.

He grabbed his phone and typed to Sylvia, the only person he knew who read medical websites for fun. "Emergency. My mucus is green. Do I need to go to the doctor and get medicine for bacteria?"

The reply came in bursts. "Whoa, slow down." Then: "My aunt's a pharmacist. She says people panic about that all the time." Then a voice message, and Michael pressed the phone to his ear.

"So the color comes from your immune cells," Sylvia said, sounding like she was reading off her hand. "They release an enzyme, and that's what makes it green or yellow. She says the color alone doesn't tell you whether it's bacteria or a virus."

Michael sat with that. He looked at the tissue again, then at the couch, then at the tissue. So the green wasn't a verdict. It was just his own body's immune cells doing their job, dyeing everything on their way through. He had been treating the color like a test result, and it wasn't one. He texted back: "So it could still just be a cold?" and Sylvia sent a thumbs up with "My aunt says exactly that."

He still didn't fully trust it, so he ran his own check. He made a chart on the back of a homework sheet: day one, clear. Day two, yellow. Day three, green. If green meant bacteria, he figured, his body should have been green from the start, since he had clearly been sick the whole time. Instead the color had arrived late, right when he was starting to feel better. That matched what Sylvia's aunt said about immune cells showing up to fight. His fever was gone. His energy was back. He was getting better, not worse.

He called Vanessa from the couch. "I'm doing the show on Friday."

"You sound stuffy," she said.

"That's just leftover green. It doesn't mean anything by itself." He crumpled the evidence into the tissue box. "I'll bring the juggling balls tomorrow. Can I borrow your extra hat, the radical one with the flames? I want the audience to remember us."

Vanessa laughed. "You can be ambassador for sick kids everywhere. Recovering but still juggling."

Michael propped the juggling balls on the armrest where he could see them, tossed one up, caught it, and grinned.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The marking 'a tempo' tells players to return to the original speed after the music has slowed down or sped up.
story:
Luca slid onto the piano bench at Samuelle's house so fast he nearly knocked the metronome off the shelf. "Okay, play it again," he said, pulling out the sheet music for "Moonlight Road," the piece their small group was performing at the school showcase in nine days. "I want to hear where I'm losing everybody."

Araya flopped onto the couch with a bag of chips. "You're losing everybody in measure twenty-four. It's like a whale deciding to take a nap mid-swim." She waved a chip for emphasis. Samuelle laughed so hard she dropped her drumsticks, and one rolled under the piano with a hollow clatter.

Luca played the passage and heard it himself this time. The music had a rit., so he slowed down, dragging the melody like a sleepy snail, but then he just kept crawling at that speed through the next eight bars while the drums and Araya's guitar chugged ahead at the normal pace. The whole thing collapsed into a lumpy pile of sound. "There!" he said. "I keep playing slow after the rit. and I never come back."

He leaned over the page, tracing the tiny markings with his finger like a detective hunting fingerprints. Right after the rit., tucked above measure twenty-six, sat two small words he'd been ignoring: a tempo. "Wait. Wait wait wait." He sat up so fast the bench squeaked. "This has to mean go back to the original speed. That's why it's sitting right there after the slow part." Araya leaned in to look, crumbs and all, and Samuelle crawled out from under the piano holding her recovered drumstick like a trophy.

"It can't be that easy," Araya said. "There's probably a rule. Ms. Bondarenko would say there's always a rule." Luca grinned. "Then it's a legitimate rule, because watch." He set his hands on the keys and played the whole passage again. This time he slowed for the rit., held the stretch for one dramatic heartbeat, and then snapped right back into the original tempo the moment he hit the marking. Samuelle came in clean on the drums, Araya's guitar locked in beside him, and suddenly the music breathed like an actual song instead of a wounded walrus.

"Yes!" Araya jumped up, scattering chips. "Do it exactly like that at the showcase and I will personally illustrate our victory in the group chat with seventeen fireworks emojis." Luca played the passage one more time, just to feel it, his fingers light and quick where they'd been heavy, and when he hit the final chord Samuelle crashed her cymbal and shouted, "Encore!"

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Researchers usually define bullying as hurtful behavior that is repeated and involves an imbalance of power, unlike a one-time argument between equals.
story:
The third time that week, Marcus took Eunice's backpack and tossed it to the kid beside him while she was tying her shoe, and the kid laughed and passed it back like they were playing some game she hadn't agreed to. Alexis watched from the swings. Eunice laughed too, but it was the wrong kind of laugh, quick and thin, the kind you use as a shield.

"That's just joking," Alexis told herself, remembering a poster from last year about bullying that she'd barely read. But something nagged at her. She tried to recall the exact words: hurtful behavior that is repeated, and involving an imbalance of power, unlike a one-time argument between equals. This was repeated, sure, every day at the playground after school. And the imbalance part, Marcus was bigger, older, and always had an audience, while Eunice stood alone. A one-time argument between equals was different, like when she and Jasmin had screamed at each other over a borrowed hoodie last spring and made up by Friday. This wasn't that. The contradiction between what Marcus called joking and what kept actually happening bothered her all through dinner.

The next day, Alexis devised a test. If it was real joking, Eunice could joke back and everyone would laugh, including Marcus. That was the rule with her friend Jasmin, who called Alexis "drip tray" for the smoothie she'd spilled in sixth grade, and Alexis called her "flagpole," and it evened out because they each had one. So at the playground, Alexis wandered over and said loudly, "Eunice, you should hide his backpack next time. Fair trade." Marcus's smile went flat. He didn't laugh. He said, "Watch it," and suddenly Eunice's backpack was back in her hands and Marcus was shooting hoops alone.

"Interesting," Alexis murmured. A real joker could take a joke. He couldn't, which meant he wasn't one.

Eunice walked over to the swings and sat down without saying anything for a minute. Then she said, "You didn't have to do that. Now he might come after you."

"Then we'll both be worth coming after," Alexis said. "Also I'm extremely competent at holding my own backpack, so you'll have backup." Eunice snorted, which turned into a real laugh this time, the slow kind. Jasmin jogged over from the monkey bars and asked what was so funny, and Alexis just pointed at Marcus, missing his shot for the third time in a row.

"There's a word for him," Eunice said quietly. "Bullying."

"Repeated," Alexis said, "with a power imbalance. Not just a one-time argument between equals. I checked."

Jasmin squinted at the court. "So what do we do about it?"

"We tell someone tomorrow, together," Alexis said. "But today..." She hopped off the swing, picked up Eunice's backpack, and held it out like a trophy. "Today, Eunice holds it herself and nobody takes it."

Eunice grabbed the strap and slung it over one shoulder, chin up, and the three of them walked past the basketball court toward the water fountain.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
