fact: Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic in 1973: people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
story:
Ray slid a newspaper across the library table with one finger, like it might bite him. "Third page. Swimmer bitten off Cape Cod. Right before our trip." He was supposed to come with Lauren's family to the coast on Saturday, and now he said he wasn't going in the water, maybe not going at all.

"You're being reckless in the other direction," Lauren said. "Staying home because of one story?" Mr. Ahmadi, shelving returns two aisles over, gave them the look he gave kids who got loud, so she lowered her voice. She went to the front desk and asked him how to retrieve old newspaper articles on the computer, and he showed her the search screen, then wandered off to help a toddler who was trying to climb the picture-book shelves.

Lauren typed in shark attack and counted. Then she typed in dog bite. Then bee sting. The screen filled up faster than she'd guessed, column after column. She tapped the glass. "Ray. Come look. If examples of shark attacks jump into your head easy, but bee stings barely do, you'll think sharks are the big danger, even when they're not. That's why the story scared you. It's easy to remember."

"Fine," Ray said, but he didn't move. Lauren kept digging and found a magazine article from years back, yellow-edged in the bound stacks. She read out loud, "Two psychologists, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, described this in 1973." She squinted at the page. "It has a name. The availability heuristic. People judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind."

"That's exactly what happened to me," Ray said. He finally came over and read the article himself, chewing the strap of his backpack. After a while he said, "Okay. I'll swim. But not at dawn, and not near seals, and that's not a negotiation, that's an amendment to the deal."

"It's not a deal, it's a beach," Lauren said, but she was already writing her source list for Monday's current events class. That was the cost of the whole afternoon; her original plan had been to finish her essay, and now the essay was untouched and the library was closing in twenty minutes. She printed one page and paid ten cents for it at the desk, and Mr. Ahmadi slid her change across the counter along with a bookmark she hadn't asked for.

Saturday morning the ocean was gray and flat, and Ray stood at the edge of the surf for a long time with his arms crossed, reading the water like it was a page he didn't trust. Then a wave caught his ankles and he yelped and grabbed Lauren's arm, laughing, and waded in up to his knees.

"First one in," he called over his shoulder, already deeper than her.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: "Agenda" is a Latin word meaning "things to be done," and a meeting agenda lists the topics in the order they will be discussed.
story:
At dinner on Tuesday, Sarah pushed her peas around her plate and finally said it out loud. "The club meeting was a disaster. We spent forty minutes arguing about snacks and never got to anything else." Her father paused with his fork halfway to his mouth. "Nobody wrote down what you were going to discuss?" Sarah blinked. That was exactly it. Zariah had wanted to talk about the river cleanup, Anouk had a plan to donate old textbooks to the library, and neither of them had said more than two sentences before the snack debate swallowed the whole room.

"Mr. Huang told me once that you write the topics down before the meeting," her mother said, ladling more soup into Sarah's bowl without being asked, because she knew Sarah forgot to eat when her mind was racing. "A list, in the order you'll take them up." Sarah nodded slowly, but something still bothered her. At the last meeting she had tried to keep order, and it hadn't worked. Why would a list change anything? She couldn't see how a piece of paper could stop six people from talking over each other. Maybe the problem wasn't the paper. Maybe the problem was that nobody, including her, knew whose turn it was next, and a list would give every topic a visible place in line.

The next day she hunted through the dictionary in the library, mostly because Zariah had laughed and called the list "a boring old word, agenda," and Sarah wanted to catch her friend being wrong for once. She found the entry and grinned. At dinner that night she announced it to her parents. "Agenda. It's a Latin word meaning things to be done." Her father laughed into his water glass. "So when Zariah says your agenda is boring, she's literally calling things that must be done boring."

She made a test of it, because an idea you haven't tested is just a wish. At Thursday's meeting she wrote three items on the whiteboard before anyone sat down: snacks, textbooks, river cleanup, in that order, snacks last. She gave each item ten minutes by the clock on the wall. When Anouk started drifting onto the subject of the bake sale, Sarah tapped the board and said, "That's not on the agenda," and Anouk sat back down, looking almost relieved. Zariah got a full five minutes on the cleanup, and two people volunteered to donate gloves and trash bags before the snack discussion even began.

The twist came at the end. When Sarah reached item three, snacks, the room went quiet, and Anouk raised her hand. "Actually, can we skip it? The meeting ran so well I don't want to wreck it with forty minutes of arguing about chips." Everyone laughed, and they voted to end early. Walking home under the streetlights, Sarah felt the brittle evening cold on her face and thought briefly about her conscience, which had pricked her at the start when she'd wondered if controlling the meeting made her bossy. Zariah bumped her shoulder. "Same agenda next month?" she asked. "Same agenda," Sarah said, and held up her crumpled list like a trophy.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: When David Rudisha set the men's 800-metre world record at the 2012 London Olympics, his first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second.
story:
The first time Audrey ran the eight hundred metres, she sprinted the whole first lap because it felt amazing to be ahead, and then the second lap swallowed her whole. Her legs turned to cement somewhere around the final bend, and Samantha passed her, and then two girls from the other school passed her, and she crossed the line in a blur of embarrassment. She walked to the fence afterward and promised herself she would figure out how the race actually worked.

That night she watched the record race from the 2012 London Olympics on her laptop, pausing it with her finger hovering over the space bar. David Rudisha ran the men's eight-hundred-metre world record that day, and she timed his laps with her phone. "His first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second," she said out loud to the empty kitchen, and she rewound and timed it again to be sure. The fastest eight-hundred-metre runner ever did not run even laps. He banked speed early, then fought to keep what was left. That felt like a hidden rule, something you could not see from the stands, and she wanted to test it on her own legs.

At the track the next afternoon, Malory was already stretching by the first lane, bouncing on her toes. "Coach says the relay spots get decided Friday," Malory said. "I want the anchor leg so bad I can taste it. Are you doing pacing work? Can I run with you?" Audrey had come to negotiate an arrangement: Malory would call out lap splits from the sideline while Audrey ran, and in exchange Audrey would help her practise baton exchanges until dark.

The first test was ugly. Audrey went out hard, hit the two-hundred mark flying, and died exactly where she had died before. "That's not it," she panted, hands on her knees. She thought about Rudisha again, about the difference between fast and reckless, and adjusted. On the next attempt she aimed for a first lap only slightly quicker than what she believed she could hold, treating the gap like a metal alloy, a blend rather than two separate metals bolted together. The first lap had to melt into the second.

The third run felt different from the inside. She rounded the bend with something still in the tank, and instead of the usual wall she found a manageable ache, and she drove through the finish line with her arms pumping. Malory jogged over waving her phone. "You negative split less, but you held on. You were three seconds faster overall."

"And you're going to be anchor," Audrey said, picking up the baton from the grass. "Come on. Hand me the stick, hit my hand, don't look back."

The sun hung low and tropical over the far bleachers as they ran the exchange again and again, two quick slaps of hand on palm echoing down the straightaway.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: Shirley Jackson's story The Lottery, published in The New Yorker in 1948, opens with children piling up stones, a detail that hints at how the lottery ends.
story:
"Read the first paragraph again," Mr. Lau said, tapping the page. "All the way back to the top."

Matteo flipped the pages of his copy of The Lottery and found the opening, the one they had skimmed two days ago. Sunny morning, flowers blooming, and the kids of the village running around while school let out for the summer. He had barely noticed it the first time. Now the ending sat in his head like a stone in his shoe.

Hawa leaned over from the next desk. "You look like the story bit you."

"It kind of did." Matteo read the paragraph again, slower this time. "Bobby Martin had a pocket full of stones, and the other boys soon had their stones." He looked up. "They were piling up stones. Right there. In paragraph one."

Elsa spun her pencil. "So? Kids collect rocks. I had a rock monopoly on my street when I was nine. Nobody touched the good ones without trading."

"Sure," Matteo said, "but this story was published in The New Yorker in 1948. Shirley Jackson put those stones there on purpose." He tapped the page twice. "It's like the author left the ending on the first page and nobody told us."

"That's foreshadowing," Hawa said. "I think."

"It is," said Mr. Lau, walking past, and kept walking, because Mr. Lau was stubborn about making them do the work themselves.

Matteo tried an experiment out loud. "If you took out the stones, paragraph one would be pure sunshine. Flowers, green grass, summer. Extravagant niceness. With the stones in it, it still sounds calm, but something's off, like a smile that's too big."

Elsa frowned at her page. "So the calm is fake?"

"Not fake," Matteo said. "The town really is calm. That's the creepy part. They pile up stones like it's a game, and at the end the stones aren't a game at all." He underlined the line in pencil. "It's a clue that only works backwards. You can't see it until you've finished."

"That's cheating," Hawa said. "Authors should warn us."

"They kind of did," Elsa said, grinning. "You just read the warning as a weather report."

Matteo wrote "stones = ending, p. 1" in his notebook, then added a question mark after it, because he wanted to ask Mr. Lau whether every object in the story was a clue or just the stones. The black box. The stool. The slips of paper. He raised his hand.

"Mr. Lau, is the black box a clue too, or do I have to sustain this level of paranoia for the rest of the year?"

Mr. Lau smiled and picked up a piece of chalk.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: A word problem can be turned into an equation: if a taxi charges 3 dollars plus 2 dollars per kilometre and a ride costs 15, then 3 + 2k = 15, so k = 6.
story:
Natalie spread the crumpled taxi receipt on the library table and smoothed it flat with her palm. "Fifteen dollars," she said. "Grandma swore the ride was only four kilometres, but the driver charged her for six. She wants to prove it before she calls the company."

Noelle leaned over the receipt. "So prove it. That's what the quiz is about tomorrow, isn't it? Mr. Nwosu's going to make us turn words into equations."

Reem pulled her chair closer and tapped the receipt with her pencil. "It says three dollars base fare plus two dollars per kilometre. I used to ride that taxi with my uncle all the time." She wrote 3 + 2k on the corner of Natalie's notebook. "The k stands for the kilometres, the thing we don't know."

Natalie stared at the letters. Under them she wrote 15, the total on the receipt, and then she sat back. "It's like a sealed box," she said slowly. "The k is hidden inside. I can't see it, but whatever I do to one side, I have to do to the other, or the balance breaks." She tried it out loud, testing the idea the way Mr. Nwosu kept telling them to. "If I take three away from the left side, I take three away from the right side too." She wrote 2k = 12 underneath.

"That's the whole algorithm," Noelle said, copying the steps into her own notebook. "Undo one thing at a time, same operation on both sides, until only the k is left."

"Then divide both sides by two," Reem said. Natalie did it, and k = 6 sat at the bottom of the page in her careful handwriting. Six kilometres. Not four, not five, but six, exactly what the driver had charged for. Somewhere in the middle of the ride they must have looped past the market, which would add the extra distance. Natalie checked it by running the equation forward: three plus two times six, which came to fifteen, which matched the receipt exactly. "Grandma was wrong," she said, almost laughing. "She's going to argue anyway."

Mr. Nwosu stopped by their table on his way to the reference shelf and glanced at the notebook. "Taxi problem?" he asked. Natalie nodded and slid the page toward him. He read it, nodded once, and said, "Good. You balanced it." He moved on without another word, and Natalie felt the warmth of that single nod spread through her whole chest.

She copied the work onto a fresh sheet for her grandmother, numbering each step so it would look official, and folded it into her backpack next to the receipt. "Six kilometres," she said again, zipping the bag shut. "She can call the company now, but they're going to tell her the same thing."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: On a graph, a simple-interest balance rises in a straight line, while a compound-interest balance curves upward, gaining more each year than the year before.
story:
Norah had spent her entire Saturday morning refilling the bulk bins at Mr. Kang's grocery store, and her pay for the day was fifty-two dollars. She slid the envelope into her backpack and biked home thinking about the jar on her dresser, the one marked NEW PHONE, into which she had already stuffed one hundred and thirty dollars.

In the kitchen, her mother was looking at a bank flyer. "They called it compound interest," her mother said. "You put money in, and it grows." Norah frowned, because her math class had just plotted two savings accounts on graph paper, and the two lines had not grown the same way at all. In Mr. Wheeler's assignment, one line rose steadily, step after step, exactly the same amount every year, while the other started close behind and then bent, climbing a little more each year than the year before, until by year five it had pulled far ahead. The steady one was simple interest. The bending one was compound.

"Can I see that?" she asked, and took the flyer to her room.

The phone she wanted cost four hundred dollars. She had one hundred and thirty, and if she added fifty dollars every month from her job, the jar would get there in about five and a half months. That was the simple way, and it felt inevitable that she would just do that. But the graph from class provoked a question she could not leave alone: if she put the money in a compound account instead, would the curve do some of the work for her?

There was a problem, though. The class graphs had covered five years, and her phone was a five-month goal. She could not see five years from here, and that was her real dilemma. So she did what Mr. Wheeler had taught them: she tested a smaller version. She took out a fresh sheet of graph paper, drew axes, and plotted her own two lines, one rising straight, one bending upward, gaining more each interval than the one before. Then she wrote five years across the bottom and stared at the gap between the lines at the end.

On Monday she found Loic stacking chairs after school. "You know how our graphs curved?" she said. "The compound one pulls away more and more the longer you leave it. So the money I'd earn in five months is tiny. But if I leave it for five years, it's a lot." Loic tilted his head. "So you're not buying the phone?" Norah laughed. "I'm buying the phone. But after that, every paycheck goes in the account, and I don't touch it. I want to be standing where the curve is."

That afternoon she rode back to Mr. Kang's store and asked if she could work Thursdays too. He checked the schedule taped behind the register, then nodded and handed her an apron. "Bins first," he said, and pointed at the oatmeal.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
story:
Julia stood on Khadija's porch holding a box of dates in her left hand, because her right hand was busy ringing the doorbell. When Khadija's grandmother opened the door, Julia passed the box over with her left hand without thinking. The grandmother took it, but Julia noticed something odd: the woman reached across herself with her right hand to receive it, and her smile went thin for just a second before warming up again.

"Come in, come in," the grandmother said, and Julia followed Khadija down the hallway, past framed photographs and the smell of coconut and lemongrass from the kitchen. Julia kept replaying that small moment on the porch. She remembered, suddenly, a flashback from school last autumn: a new student from Indonesia had handed Mr. Brown a permission slip, and Mr. Brown had joked, "Right hand, right on," and the boy had laughed and said, "In Indonesia and Malaysia, we use the right hand for eating and for giving and receiving things." Julia had assumed he was only talking about himself. Now, watching Khadija's family, she wondered if the rule ran through the whole household, invisible like a current under still water.

At dinner, the table crowded with dishes, Julia tested her idea. She kept her eyes low and her hands still, and she watched. Khadija tore flatbread with her right hand. Her father spooned curry with his right. Her little brother reached for the water pitcher with his left, and Khadija's mother caught his wrist and steered it across to the right, saying nothing, as if correcting a wobble in a beginner cyclist. Nobody said the rule out loud. It was just there, the way the rule at Julia's own house was that you took off your shoes at the door and that elbows never touched the table, rules her friends always got wrong the first time.

When the bowl of rice came around, Julia passed it with her right hand, careful and deliberate. The grandmother looked at her, really looked, and nodded once. "You noticed," she said. Julia felt her ears go hot. Khadija leaned over and whispered, "It's a sign of respect. Grandma will talk about you for a week now."

Later, when the plates were cleared, Khadija's father mentioned that they were hoping to buy the house next door, if the mortgage on it wasn't too heavy, and that the neighbors' moving sale seemed imminent. Khadija pulled Julia out to the porch to look at the fireflies. "You know, when I went to your house, I gave your mom my gift with my right hand and she took it with her left," Khadija said. "Did I insult her?"

Julia thought about her mother, who waved hello with whichever hand was free. "I don't think she even noticed," she said.

Khadija frowned at the fireflies. "So it matters here and not there," she said. "How do you know which place you're in?"

Julia watched a light blink on and off above the hedge. "Maybe you just watch, like I did tonight," she said. "Or maybe you get it wrong first."

"Getting it wrong sounds terrible," said Khadija.

Julia laughed. "It's only a hand."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Specific details, like 'Grandma's red bicycle' instead of 'a bike', give an improv partner more to build on.
story:
Nicolas stood in the wings of the community theatre, holding a slip of paper that read "beach trip" and wishing he had never signed up for the improv workshop. The empty stage intimidated him more than any audience ever had, because on stage you couldn't hide behind a script. Ms. De Vries clapped her hands and explained the rule: whatever your partner says, you accept it and add to it. "Yes, and," she said. "That's the whole game."

His first scene, with Adnan, fell apart in thirty seconds. "We're at the beach," Nicolas offered, and Adnan said, "Yes, and we brought some stuff." They passed an invisible box back and forth, calling it "things" and "supplies," until neither of them knew what to do next. The audience of other kids giggled in the embarrassed way that means they were glad it wasn't them. Renee, sitting in the front row, wasn't giggling. She wanted the funniest scene of the afternoon, because the two funniest people got to perform at the spring showcase, and she already had a bit about a seagull she was saving for it.

Backstage, Nicolas turned the failed scene over in his mind. Adnan had said "some stuff," and the scene had died. In the scene before theirs, a girl had said "Grandma's red bicycle," and suddenly her partner was ringing the bell and yelling about the busted brake. It wasn't talent, he decided. It was the words themselves. Vague words gave you nothing, but specific words, like "Grandma's red bicycle" instead of "a bike," gave your partner something real to grab. He tested the idea quietly, mouthing beach words until he found a sharp one.

"Renee, go with me this time," he whispered, and she shrugged like it cost her something, seagull bit and all. On stage, Nicolas began immediately. "Yes, and the estuary we're wading in is full of crabs," he said, "and one of them has my grandmother's wedding ring in its claw." Renee's eyes lit up. "Yes, and the crab speaks French," she said, "and he'll trade the ring for a croissant." Nicolas dug in his pocket and produced an imaginary croissant so warm he described the butter dripping. The kids in the audience were laughing for real now, leaning forward, and Adnan shouted from the front row that he wanted to be the crab's lawyer.

Ms. De Vries watched with her arms folded and a small smile, and when the scene ended she said, "Nicolas, that was eloquent for a guy wrestling a crustacean." Renee grabbed his sleeve. "Showcase," she said. "You and me. Crabs and everything."

Nicolas bowed, and the paper slip reading "beach trip" drifted out of his pocket and landed on the stage boards like a dropped ticket.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: The PG-13 movie rating was introduced in the United States on July 1, 1984, as a step between PG and R.
story:
The park benches were sticky with humid air, and Michael kept wiping his palms on his jeans while he waited by the fountain. His first actual date. Leah was meeting him here in ten minutes, and the plan was simple: walk through the park, then catch a movie at the theater on the far side. The problem was which movie.

Jaiveer had come along to keep him company until Leah arrived, and now he was being Jaiveer about it. "You can't just say 'let's see a movie,'" he said, elaborating with his hands the way he did when he thought something was obvious. "You have to already know what you're both allowed to see. That's consumer research. My sister calls it that."

Michael frowned at the fountain. He had never wondered about movie ratings before. They had just always been there, stamped on posters and trailers like weather. But now it mattered, because half the movies playing were rated one thing and half another, and he only had a ten-dollar bill and one shot at this. Was there even a rule? PG meant kids could go, R meant they couldn't, but what about everything squeezed in between? He tried to remember anything his dad had said and came up with nothing.

"Wait," he said slowly. "There's a middle one. I've seen the tag on trailers. Between PG and R."

"You mean PG-13?"

Michael pulled out his phone and searched for it, scrolling fast, because Leah's bus stopped at the corner in five minutes and a plan without a movie was no plan at all. He read the result twice. "It says here the PG-13 movie rating was introduced in the United States on July 1, 1984. A whole separate rating, added right between PG and R." He looked up. "That's why it exists. Somebody put it there."

"So you're saying there's a whole rating that exists just for movies like this one?" Jaiveer squinted at the theater marquee across the park, where the titles gleamed in the haze. "Then that's your answer. If the movie's PG-13, you're fine."

Michael tested the idea against the marquee, matching letters to ratings, until he found one that worked for both of them and started at the right time. He had just worked it out when he heard the bus hiss to a stop behind him.

He turned around, and Leah was already waving.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, 'yes, and' means accepting what your partner has established (yes) and then adding something new to it (and).
story:
Landon's grandfather had turned the sunroom into a stage of sorts: two folding chairs, a lamp on a crate, and a notebook full of writing prompts. Landon and Alistair had come to practise before Monday's drama camp audition, because the director was going to pair them up and make them improvise a scene with no script at all.

"We're a spaceship crew," Alistair said, launching in. "The engine's broken."

Landon crossed his arms. "No we're not. We're knights."

Alistair tried again. "Fine, knights. Our castle is under siege."

"No, it isn't."

The scene collapsed. Alistair sat down on one of the folding chairs and spun the notebook toward Landon. "We're doing it wrong. The good campers do something and I can't tell what it is. I've been trying to infer it from watching the older kids, but every scene I watch, all I notice is they never argue."

Landon flipped through the notebook. His grandfather had written notes from an acting class he took in 1974, back when the neighbourhood was affluent enough to have its own little theatre. One line was circled twice: "Yes, and." Landon read it, then read the scribble beside it. "It's called 'yes, and,'" he said slowly. "You say yes to whatever your partner set up, then you add something."

"Add something how?"

"Like this." Landon stood and gestured at the lamp. "Alistair, this lighthouse is ours, and the bulb just died."

Alistair's shoulders came up. "Yes, and there's a ship coming toward the rocks right now."

"Yes, and I think the keeper's old flare gun still works."

"Yes, and it's in the flooded cellar." Alistair grabbed an umbrella from the coat rack and held it like a torch. He waded across an imaginary cellar, and Landon could hear him breathing harder, the way he only did when a game was working. They built the scene for ten straight minutes: the flare, the ship, a sailor with a broken arm carried up the stairs.

When they finally stopped, Landon understood what he'd been missing before. Saying no had been a signal to Alistair that his ideas were worthless, so Alistair stopped offering any, and the scene starved. Every "yes, and" handed his friend a new brick, and his friend kept building.

They ran it three more times, trading who started. On the last round Alistair opened with, "We're two guys in a sunroom, and the audition is in two days." Landon picked up the flare gun umbrella and aimed it at the window. "Yes, and we're going to be ready."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: To ask for the bill in French, you say "L'addition, s'il vous plaît," meaning "The bill, please."
story:
Aurora had a green notebook full of French phrases, and by Saturday morning she had crossed out three of them. "Un croissant, s'il vous plaît" had worked fine at the bakery on Rue Vernet in her imagination, but asking for the bill had gone wrong twice. She'd written "La note, s'il vous plaît" first, because "la note" sounded like a bill to her, and then "La facture," which her dictionary said meant an invoice. Neither felt like something a waiter would actually say, and the restaurant test was Monday night at Chez Margot, where Ms. Kaminski had booked a table for the whole class.

Martin flopped onto her kitchen floor with his own notebook. "I've got the food part down," he said. "Croque-monsieur, salade, une limonade. It's the money part that scares me. What if I just hold out my wallet and point?"

"Then you'd survive," Aurora said, "but you'd look like a tourist." She flipped her laptop toward him and opened a video of a French family finishing dinner in a real bistro. She'd decided to test an idea: if "la note" and "la facture" were wrong, some other word had to be right, and it ought to show up in real restaurant scenes. She watched the waiter's hands, not his mouth, then played the clip again with the sound magnified.

That was when she caught it. The waiter set down the small tray, and the man at the table said something quick and polite. Aurora backed the video up, listened three times, and wrote it down carefully: "L'addition, s'il vous plaît." She found two more videos, and in both of them, there it was again, the same phrase, every single time. Not "la note." Not "la facture." "L'addition." She underlined it twice, and Martin leaned over her shoulder to copy it, muttering it under his breath like a spell.

Lina arrived at Monday's dinner rehearsal still shaking her head. "I practiced 'la note' all weekend," she said, "because my cousin in Montreal told me that's what she says." But when the waiter came, Lina went first anyway, took a breath, and said, "L'addition, s'il vous plaît." The waiter smiled and brought the tray without a single confused blink, and Lina turned back to the table with her arms up like she'd scored a goal.

Aurora ordered last, all the way through: "Un croque-monsieur et une limonade, s'il vous plaît." When the plates were cleared she looked straight at the waiter and said the phrase she'd dug out of all those videos. He nodded, and a moment later the little tray appeared in front of her with the paper bill folded on top. Ms. Kaminski, watching from the end of the table, raised her water glass. "Well," she said. "The verdict is in, and I think you all just paid for your own dinners. In French."

Martin slipped his copy of the phrase into his shirt pocket for next time. "Chez Margot," he said, "won't know what hit them."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: To finish 800 metres in three minutes on a 400-metre track, a runner must average 90 seconds for each lap.
story:
Jack stood at the white line of the running track with a race number safety-pinned to his shirt and a problem he could not stop turning over. In three weeks he had to run eight hundred metres in under three minutes to make the county team, but every time he tried, the first lap felt wonderful and the second lap felt like wading through wet sand. Ms. Malik had watched him last Tuesday and said nothing except, "Think about where your legs go before they go there." Jack had a suspicion the trouble was invisible, hiding somewhere between his stopwatch and his enthusiasm.

He flipped his race number over on the bus and worked it out with a pencil stub borrowed from Emil. Eight hundred metres was two laps of the four-hundred-metre track. Three minutes was one hundred eighty seconds. He wrote it small, then smaller, and the answer arrived on the paper like something that had been waiting: to finish eight hundred metres in three minutes, he had to average ninety seconds for each lap. Not one number, but the same number twice. Emil leaned over his shoulder and read it aloud, then checked it with his fingers, counting the seconds in tens.

The next morning King held the stopwatch at the line. "Ninety seconds, then ninety more," Jack said. "If I come through the first lap fast, slow me down. Yell if you have to." King nodded and clicked the watch. Jack went out, and the hard part was that the first lap felt terrible on purpose, like holding a horse back at a gate. He wanted to fly. Instead he complied with the number on the paper, watching King's raised hand at the two-hundred-metre mark, where a small crowd of walkers had gathered by the fence.

He crossed the line for lap one at ninety-one seconds. King shouted it, and Jack felt a strange calm settle over him, because now the second lap was a race he could actually win. He pushed hard up the back straight, and on the final bend he found something left, a vigorous burst that carried him past the imaginary runner he was always chasing. King clicked the watch. Two minutes, fifty-two seconds. Eight seconds to spare. Jack lay on the infield grass, laughing at the clouds.

Emil jogged over holding the race number. "There's a problem," he said slowly. "You pinned this on upside down this morning. Look at the back." Jack took it. Under his pencil marks, in printed ink he had never noticed, was a small chart of suggested splits, and next to it a line saying the target pace for his age group had been changed this season to three minutes and two seconds, not three minutes flat. His pencil math had been aimed at a time nobody had asked him for.

Jack sat up and looked down the track, empty now except for the walkers drifting away. Three weeks until the race, and two different numbers in his head. He turned the paper over and over, then folded it into his pocket and stood. "Same time tomorrow," he said. "Bring the stopwatch."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: Smokey Bear's campfire rule is drown, stir, drown again, then feel for heat, because if a campfire is too hot to touch, it is too hot to leave.
story:
Anais had been on the Miller's Creek trail exactly four times in her life, and today she was pretending it was practice for the wilderness. "Two miles," she announced to Tenley, who was hiking beside her with a granola bar already half gone. "That's nothing. Camp Wanderhawk is a whole week of trails like this. Real ones, with bears."

"Bears," Kiaan repeated from behind them, delighted. "Probably just raccoons."

"Raccoons can thrive anywhere," Anais said. "Bears need real forest. That's the difference." She was carrying a daypack loaded with everything she'd packed and repacked three times last night: flashlight, water bottle, the laminated list her mom had printed, and one notebook where she planned to record every skill she learned before camp even started.

That was why she'd begged Mr. Kim to come along. He lived two houses down, and he hiked this trail every Saturday, and once, a long time ago, he had been a camp counselor himself. Today he had promised them lunch at the creek and one demonstration.

At the gravel clearing by the water, he set down his pack and got out a small shovel, a bucket, and a single match. "Sit," he said. "You wanted lessons. Lesson one happens before any fire ever starts."

He built a fire no bigger than a dinner plate, and they roasted the last of the marshmallows Tenley had smuggled in. When the flames had died to grey coals, Mr. Kim kicked a little dirt over the pile and stood up. "There," he said. "Out. Let's pack up."

Kiaan reached for the bucket, but Anais stopped him. Something wasn't right. She crouched at the edge of the fire ring and stared at the ashes. The smoke had stopped, sure, but the wind kept shifting one thin feather of it back up, in a pattern, like the pile was still breathing underneath. Dirt on top could hide heat. That was the whole trick of it.

"It's not out," she said. "I think the middle's still hot under the dirt. We can't see it, so we have to test it another way."

Mr. Kim folded his arms, but he was smiling. "Go on, then."

Anais remembered a poster from the ranger station at the trailhead, the one with the bear in the ranger hat. She'd read it twice while waiting for Tenley to tie her shoe. "Drown, stir, drown again," she said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "Then feel for heat. If it's too hot to touch, it's too hot to leave." She grabbed the bucket, sloshed the whole thing over the coals, and stirred the black mess with the shovel until it looked like soup, then dumped her water bottle over it too.

"Now the touching part." She waved her palm slowly above the wet ash. Warm. She waited, waved again. Warm, but less. A third time, and her hand stayed still. Cool. "Cold," she reported. "Cold all the way through. Now it's actually out."

"And that," Mr. Kim said, "is the one rule they'll drill into you at Wanderhawk until your whole cabin can say it in one coherent sentence. Fire safety has a hierarchy, and feeling for heat is at the top of it."

Anais wrote it in her notebook in big letters, underlined twice, and drew a small bear in a hat beside it. She was going to be the kid in her cabin who already knew everything. She jogged to catch up with the others on the trail, notebook bouncing against her hip, already planning what she'd teach them first.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
story:
Alexis spread two boxes of cereal on the picnic table in his backyard: Sparkle O's, the name brand, and Round Marts, the store brand his mom bought to save money. His science fair project was due in nine days, and he had a question he actually wanted answered. Did people really taste a difference, or did they just taste the box?

Bodie arrived first, riding his bike over the gravel alley and skidding to a stop by the fence. Youcef came next, carrying a notebook and a pen he clicked constantly. "So we're the taste testers?" Bodie asked, already reaching for a box. Alexis pulled both boxes away and carried them inside. When he came back, he held a tray with four bowls, each labeled with a letter on masking tape: A, B, A, B. Youcef wrote the letters down.

"Wait," Bodie said. "Which one is the expensive one?" Alexis shook his head. "That's the whole point. If I tell you, you'll say the name brand tastes better because you think it should." He had read about it in his library book the night before, sitting at the kitchen table long after his mom had told him to sleep. The book called it a blind test, because the people tested don't know which sample is which, so their expectations can't sway their answers. That exact sentence had made him sit up straight. He explained it in one line: "It's a blind test. You don't know which bowl is which, so you can't be biased."

Bodie ate a spoonful from A, then B, then A again, frowning like the frown itself was data. "B is better. B tastes more like actual oats." Youcef tasted both and chose A. Alexis recorded every answer, plus three more from neighbors who wandered over when they smelled cereal in the backyard, and by evening he had eleven results. Nine of the eleven picked the store brand, or the name brand, or said they were identical, and when Alexis finally revealed which letters matched which boxes, even he was surprised. Bodie had chosen the cheap one. Bodie, who swore up and down that Sparkle O's were the only cereal worth eating.

"You tricked me," Bodie said, but he was grinning. Ms. Hamdan, the neighbor whose garden ran along the back fence, had been one of the eleven, and she called across the rows of tomato plants, "Would it be a privilege to see your results at the fair? I'd like to know if my own answers fooled me too." Alexis said it would, and he meant it.

That night he taped his data sheet to the garage wall, all eleven rows of letters and choices, and thought about how the answer had been hiding inside people the whole time, invisible until he covered the boxes. Nine days was still enough time to test soda, and maybe chocolate chips, and Bodie had already volunteered to comply with any future experiment involving snacks. Alexis pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward him and wrote at the top: Experiment Two.
